title: Geography at Royal Crest: Reading the sky
_note: say = text sent to ElevenLabs (numbers spelled out where they must be read a certain way); cap = on-screen caption. TEN uses 'Stacy – Warm South African' from the account's voice list; swap voice_id for any voice in your account.

lines.say: Every morning at nine, a student at Royal Crest walks out to a small white box on the grass.
lines.cap: Every morning at nine, a student at Royal Crest walks out to a small white box on the grass.

lines.say: A box? What's inside it?
lines.cap: A box? What’s inside it?

lines.say: The weather. Today we read it, then we fly up into the clouds to see where our rain comes from.
lines.cap: The weather. Today we read it, then we fly up into the clouds to see where our rain comes from.

lines.say: Welcome to the weather station at Royal Crest Academy, in Bikita. O Level Geography, for ZIMSEC and Cambridge.
lines.cap: Welcome to the weather station at Royal Crest Academy, in Bikita. O Level Geography, for ZIMSEC and Cambridge.

lines.say: Lesson one. Siting the station. Open, flat ground, on short grass, well away from buildings and trees.
lines.cap: Lesson one: siting the station. Open, flat ground, on short grass, well away from buildings and trees.

lines.say: The rule is distance: at least twice the height of anything nearby. A ten metre tree means twenty metres away.
lines.cap: The rule is distance: at least twice the height of anything nearby. A 10 m tree means 20 m away.

lines.say: So the trees can't shade it or block the wind.
lines.cap: So the trees can’t shade it or block the wind.

lines.say: Lesson two. The Stevenson screen. White, to reflect the sun. Louvred sides, so air flows through but sunlight can't get in.
lines.cap: Lesson two: the Stevenson screen. White, to reflect the sun. Louvred sides, so air flows through but sunlight can’t get in.

lines.say: It stands on legs, so the thermometers sit between one and a quarter and two metres above the grass.
lines.cap: It stands on legs, so the thermometers sit 1.25 to 2 m above the grass.

lines.say: Wait. Which way does the door face?
lines.cap: Wait. Which way does the door face?

lines.say: Here in Zimbabwe, south. For most of the year our sun is in the northern sky, so a south-facing door keeps sunlight off the thermometers when we open it. In Britain, the books say north.
lines.cap: Here in Zimbabwe, south. For most of the year our sun is in the northern sky, so a south-facing door keeps sunlight off the thermometers when we open it. In Britain, the books say north.

lines.say: Inside, Six's thermometer. Two small markers are pushed up and down, and stay at the highest and lowest temperatures since yesterday. A magnet resets them.
lines.cap: Inside: Six’s thermometer. Two small markers stay at the highest and lowest temperatures since yesterday. A magnet resets them.

lines.say: Beside it, the wet and dry bulb thermometers. Water evaporating from the wet bulb cools it. The bigger the difference, the drier the air.
lines.cap: Beside it, the wet and dry bulb thermometers. Water evaporating from the wet bulb cools it. The bigger the difference, the drier the air.

lines.say: Lesson three. The calculations you'll see in the exam. Today's maximum, thirty-one degrees. Minimum, fifteen.
lines.cap: Lesson three: the exam calculations. Today’s maximum: 31 °C. Minimum: 15 °C.

lines.say: The daily range is the difference: sixteen degrees. The daily mean is the average: twenty-three degrees.
lines.cap: Daily range = 31 − 15 = 16 °C. Daily mean = (31 + 15) ÷ 2 = 23 °C.

lines.say: Dry bulb, twenty-four. Wet bulb, nineteen. A difference of five. The table gives the relative humidity: about sixty percent.
lines.cap: Dry bulb 24 °C, wet bulb 19 °C, difference 5. From the table: relative humidity about 60%.

lines.say: Sixty percent. So the air is holding more than half the water it could.
lines.cap: 60%. So the air is holding more than half the water it could.

lines.say: Lesson four. Wind and rain. The wind vane points to where the wind comes from. A wind from the east is an easterly.
lines.cap: Lesson four: wind and rain. The wind vane points to where the wind comes from. A wind from the east is an easterly.

lines.say: The anemometer's cups spin faster as the wind gets stronger. The standard height for both is ten metres, so a school mast is a compromise.
lines.cap: The anemometer’s cups spin faster as the wind gets stronger. The standard height for both is 10 m, so a school mast is a compromise.

lines.say: The rain gauge stands thirty centimetres above the ground, so rain can't splash in. We plot a month of wind on a wind rose.
lines.cap: The rain gauge stands 30 cm above the ground, so rain can’t splash in. We plot a month of wind on a wind rose.

lines.say: Okay. Now the fun part. Let's fly.
lines.cap: Okay. Now the fun part. Let’s fly.

lines.say: Lesson five. A hot summer afternoon in Bikita. The ground heats the air above it. Warm air is lighter, so it rises, in currents called thermals.
lines.cap: Lesson five: a hot summer afternoon in Bikita. The ground heats the air above it. Warm air is lighter, so it rises, in currents called thermals.

lines.say: As it rises, it cools, about ten degrees for every kilometre. At the dew point, water vapour condenses into tiny droplets. A cloud is born.
lines.cap: As it rises, it cools, about 10 °C for every kilometre. At the dew point, water vapour condenses into tiny droplets. A cloud is born.

lines.say: Wait. We're inside the cloud now!
lines.cap: Wait. We’re inside the cloud now!

lines.say: Cumulus grows into cumulonimbus, a thunderstorm cloud that can tower higher than Mount Everest. Droplets and ice crystals grow until they're heavy enough to fall as rain.
lines.cap: Cumulus grows into cumulonimbus, a thunderstorm cloud that can tower higher than Mount Everest. Droplets and ice crystals grow until they’re heavy enough to fall as rain.

lines.say: That's convectional rain, and it brings about nine tenths of Zimbabwe's rain, from November to March.
lines.cap: That’s convectional rain, and it brings about 90% of Zimbabwe’s rain, from November to March.

lines.say: Relief rain falls when moist winds rise over mountains, like our Eastern Highlands. Frontal rain falls where warm and cold air meet.
lines.cap: Relief rain falls when moist winds rise over mountains, like our Eastern Highlands. Frontal rain falls where warm and cold air meet.

lines.say: And nimbostratus: a thick, dark grey layer that hides the sun and brings steady rain for hours.
lines.cap: And nimbostratus: a thick, dark grey layer that hides the sun and brings steady rain for hours.

lines.say: Lesson six. Reading the sky. We name the cloud, and count the cover in oktas, eighths of the sky. Zero is clear. Eight is overcast.
lines.cap: Lesson six: reading the sky. We name the cloud and count the cover in oktas, eighths of the sky. 0 is clear. 8 is overcast.

lines.say: So today, five oktas of cumulus.
lines.cap: So today: 5 oktas of cumulus.

lines.say: But why record all this every day?
lines.cap: But why record all this every day?

lines.say: Because data saves lives. In America, school rain gauges in the CoCoRaHS network have helped forecasters issue flood warnings.
lines.cap: Because data saves lives. In America, school rain gauges in the CoCoRaHS network have helped forecasters issue flood warnings.

lines.say: NASA's GLOBE programme checks students' cloud reports against satellites. In Britain, schools use their station to compare microclimates.
lines.cap: NASA’s GLOBE programme checks students’ cloud reports against satellites. In Britain, schools use their station to compare microclimates.

lines.say: And here, farmers ask one question every season: when will the rains come? Our records help answer it.
lines.cap: And here, farmers ask one question every season: when will the rains come? Our records help answer it.

lines.say: This is Education Five Point Zero. Teaching, research, community service, innovation and industrialisation, rooted in our heritage. Our climate is part of that heritage.
lines.cap: This is Education 5.0. Teaching, research, community service, innovation and industrialisation, rooted in our heritage. Our climate is part of that heritage.

lines.say: So a white box on the grass is a research lab.
lines.cap: So a white box on the grass is a research lab.

lines.say: And where does it lead, for a child from Bikita?
lines.cap: And where does it lead, for a child from Bikita?

lines.say: Meteorology and Climate Science at the University of Zimbabwe. Geography, and GIS and earth observation, at universities across the country, including Great Zimbabwe University in Masvingo.
lines.cap: Meteorology and Climate Science at the University of Zimbabwe. Geography, and GIS and earth observation, at universities across the country, including Great Zimbabwe University in Masvingo.

lines.say: Then careers as a forecaster at the Meteorological Services Department, a hydrologist, an agricultural extension officer, an environmental officer, a GIS analyst, or in disaster management.
lines.cap: Then careers as a forecaster at the Meteorological Services Department, a hydrologist, an agricultural extension officer, an environmental officer, a GIS analyst, or in disaster management.

lines.say: At Royal Crest, it starts in Form One. Geography with a working weather station, alongside the sciences, for ZIMSEC and Cambridge.
lines.cap: At Royal Crest, it starts in Form 1. Geography with a working weather station, alongside the sciences, for ZIMSEC and Cambridge.

lines.say: Science. Innovation. Skill.
lines.cap: Science. Innovation. Skill.

lines.cap: Parents: Form 1 places for January 2027 are limited.

lines.cap: Come and read the sky with us.
